chunks.document_content: Keywords Diabetic macular edema, Topical NSAIDs, BCVA, CMT ​Introduction Background Diabetes Mellitus (DM) is one of the most common chronic diseases worldwide and poses significant chal­ lenges to patient health. In 2021, the worldwide preva­ lence of diabetes in 20-79 years old adults was reported to be 10.5% (536.6 million people) and is expected to rise to 12.2% (783.2 million people) in 2045 [1]. Objective In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we aimed to compare the outcomes of using topical NSAIDs in patients with DME, both as stand-alone therapy and as an adjunct to other treatment modalities. Methods This systematic review was performed according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) [10]. Studies pertaining to the treatment diabetic macular edema using NSAIDS ver­ sus anti-VEGF were reviewed and screened, with those matching the pre-determined eligibility criteria selected and further analyzed. In patients with uncontrolled diabetes, persistent hyperglycemia causes long-term vascular damage to sev­ eral organs, resulting in macrovascular and microvascu­ lar complications. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is the most common microvascular complication in patients with diabetes, with an estimated global prevalence of 191 mil­ lion patients by 2030 [2]. The primary outcome of this study was improvement in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA). Secondary out­ comes included central macular thickness (CMT), macu­ lar volume, and treatment complications. DR is classified into two stages: non-proliferative dia­ betic retinopathy (NPDR) and proliferative diabetic reti­ nopathy (PDR). NPDR is the early stage of DR, in which key features include the formation of microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMAs). PDR is characterized by neovas­ cularization, which can lead to various vision-threatening complications. In addition, patients may develop diabetic macular edema (DME) at any stage of DR [3]. Eligibility criteria All clinical trials that compared the use of NSAIDs with other agents in patients with DME were included. Indi­ viduals of all ages, sexes, races, ethnicities, and comor­ bidity statuses were included. The exclusion criteria included studies that were not performed in humans, studies that were predominantly focused on other dia­ betic ocular pathologies, studies that mainly focused on the use of NSAIDs after cataract surgery, the use of intravitreal NSAIDs, and studies that were conducted on a cohort not representative of the general patient popu­ lation. After conducting a literature search, 68 published studies were reviewed using this eligibility criteria, with 62 studies excluded, yielding only 6 studies qualifying for inclusion in this review. DME is a common complication of diabetes and one of the leading causes of significant vision loss globally. Chronic hyperglycemia and retinal hypoxia stimulate the production of VEGF, resulting in vascular hyperper­ meability with intra- and subretinal thickening, which results in the development of DME [4, 5]. Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections are considered the first-line treatment in the management of DME [5]. Some disadvantages of the use of such agents include the need for re-injection, short-term effects, and the risk of complications. Search strategy and selection of studies The literature search was conducted using several medi­ cal databases, to search for relevant articles published on the topic.

chunks.document_content: The severity stage of diabetic retinopathy (e.g., non-proliferative versus pro­ liferative diabetic retinopathy) was also not consistently available in the retrospective records and therefore could not be incorporated into the analysis. Because retinopa­ thy severity may influence ischemic burden, treatment The treatment burden associated with anti-VEGF therapy remains a major challenge in the management of DME. Frequent intravitreal injections and clinic vis­ its can negatively affect patient adherence and long-term treatment persistence. Previous studies have demon­ strated that non-adherence and irregular follow-up are associated with poorer visual outcomes [9]. In this con­ text, the moderate injection frequency observed in our study likely reflects a balance between treatment efficacy and real-world constraints, including healthcare system capacity and patient compliance. Structural retinal factors may also contribute to vari­ ability in treatment response. Biomarkers such as disor­ ganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL) and disruption of the ellipsoid zone have been shown to be associated with limited visual recovery despite ongoing anti-VEGF therapy [15, 16]. Although these parameters were not evaluated in the present study, they may partly explain the lack of an independent association between injection number and visual outcomes. Emerging therapeutic strategies aim to reduce treat­ ment burden while maintaining efficacy. Approaches such as treat-and-extend regimens and longer-acting anti-VEGF agents have shown promise in reducing injec­ tion frequency while preserving visual outcomes [17, 18]. However, their comparative effectiveness in real-world settings may vary depending on patient characteristics, adherence, and healthcare system factors, and further requirements, and visual prognosis, its absence limits assessment of disease heterogeneity within the cohort. Structural and quantitative OCT biomarkers, includ­ ing disorganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL), ellip­ soid zone disruption, central retinal thickness, and fluid compartment characteristics, were also not evaluated. Because retreatment and treatment-switching decisions in routine clinical practice were substantially guided by OCT findings, the absence of these parameters may have influenced both physician decision-making and observed visual outcomes, thereby introducing additional unmea­ sured confounding. This also limits mechanistic inter­ pretation of the relationship between anatomical and functional outcomes. Moreover, functional outcomes beyond best-corrected visual acuity, such as contrast sensitivity, reading performance, and vision-related qual­ ity of life, were not routinely available in the retrospec­ tive records and therefore could not be evaluated. As a result, reliance on BCVA alone may incompletely reflect the broader functional impact of diabetic macular edema or the real-world patient-centered benefits of treatment. Finally, although efforts were made to include complete datasets, potential missing or unrecorded data for certain variables cannot be entirely excluded, which may repre­ sent an additional source of bias.

chunks.document_content: Keywords Diabetic macular edema, Topical NSAIDs, BCVA, CMT studies were selected for this review based on their over­ all quality and relevance. The flowchart in Fig. 1 displays the process of selecting studies for this review [10]. Study selection and data extraction Two independent researchers reviewed all studies and excluded articles using the pre-set inclusion and exclu­ sion criteria. After thorough search using 5 databases, 68 articles were originally identified. With further exami­ nation of the studies using the criteria and removing duplicates, 46 studies were ineligible. Of the remaining 22 studies, 12 were further excluded due to failure of meeting the set criteria. Finally, the remaining 10 stud­ ies underwent a thorough review, with a total of 6 studies included for definitive inclusion as they met all pre-req­ uisites set. Any discrepancies between the chosen stud­ ies were discussed between the two researchers, and if not resolved, the studies were sent to a third researcher to independently assess and decide if they should be included. The data from each study was then extracted and inputted into a defined Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Description of studies A summary of the baseline characteristics of the studies included in this systematic review is shown in the table of Fig. 2. The total sample size was 446 (892 eyes). Most of the studies had the same intervention performed for both eyes of the same patient, apart from one article, Evli­ yaoglu et al., where in each patient, one eye was treated with the intervention and one with the control [7]. Four of the studies were randomized controlled trials, one was a pilot study and one was a retrospective observational study. The intervention in these studies was the addi­ tion of topical NSAIDs, with control groups consisting of either placebo (Friedman et al.), intravitreal anti-VEGF monotherapy (Gabr et al., Nikkhah et al., Mohan et al.), or no intervention (Evliyoglu et al.). The follow up time was varied between the studies. Gabr et al. and Nikkhah et al. reported 6 month follow up outcomes [6, 8]. Evli­ yoglu et al. had a follow up time of 6 weeks [7]. Whereas, Friedman et al. and Mohan et al. had the longest follow up time at 12 months compared to Pinna et al. with the shortest follow up [9, 13, 14]. Of these studies, three were suitable for meta-analysis with comparable data allowing for further analysis. Data synthesis After collecting the data, the authors assessed whether pooling of the results was considered feasible based on the individual outcomes and if it was reported by more than two studies. The mean difference was used to report continuous data and the odds ratio was used for dichot­ omous data. Odds ratios were chosen to provide a con­ sistent and easily interpretable effect measure across studies with different baseline risks, which was especially important given the heterogeneity of DME outcomes in this review. Statistical analysis was done by using 'Review Manager' and results was presented in forest plots with 95% confidence intervals.
